    Unique Continuation

    Setting and statement

    Edit

    Throughout, \((M,g)\) is a connected Riemannian manifold of dimension \(n\), not necessarily complete. All bundles are real; for Hermitian bundles replace \(\la\cdot,\cdot\ra\) by \(\operatorname{Re}\la\cdot,\cdot\ra\) everywhere. We write \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) for a local orthonormal frame, \(e^1,\dots,e^n\) for the dual coframe, and \(\la u,v\ra=\int_M\la u,v\ra\dd\vol\), \(\norm u^2=\la u,u\ra\) for \(L^2\)-quantities.

    Definition (Dirac bundle)
    Edit

    A Dirac bundle over \(M\) is a Euclidean vector bundle \(\cS\to M\) with a metric connection \(\nabla\) and a bundle map \(c\colon T^*M\to\operatorname{End}(\cS)\) (Clifford multiplication) such that for all \(1\)-forms \(\alpha,\beta\):

    1. \(c(\alpha)c(\beta)+c(\beta)c(\alpha)=-2\,g(\alpha,\beta)\,\mathrm{Id}\);

    2. \(c(\alpha)^*=-c(\alpha)\) pointwise;

    3. \(\nabla_X\big(c(\alpha)u\big)=c(\nabla_X\alpha)u+c(\alpha)\nabla_Xu\).

    Its Dirac operator is \(Du=\sum_{i}c(e^i)\nabla_{e_i}u\); this does not depend on the frame.

    By (a)-(b), \(c(\alpha)^*c(\alpha)=-c(\alpha)^2=|\alpha|^2\); so \(c(\alpha)\) is an isometry when \(|\alpha|=1\), and then \(c(\alpha)^{-1}=-c(\alpha)\).

    In local coordinates, write

    \[ \alpha=\frac1{p!}\alpha_{i_1\cdots i_p} \,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p}, \]

    \[ \beta=\frac1{p!}\beta_{j_1\cdots j_p} \,dx^{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{j_p}. \]

    Using the inverse metric \(g^{ij}\), define

    \[ \beta^{i_1\cdots i_p} = g^{i_1j_1}\cdots g^{i_pj_p} \beta_{j_1\cdots j_p}. \]

    Recall, by definition, \(\beta^\sharp\) is the unique vector field satisfying

    \begin{equation} g(\beta^\sharp,X)=\beta(X) \end{equation}

    for every vector field \(X\). The corresponding \(p\)-vector is

    \[ \beta^\sharp = \frac1{p!}\beta^{i_1\cdots i_p} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_1}} \wedge\cdots\wedge \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{i_p}}. \]

    In particular,

    \[ (dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p}) \left( \partial_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge\partial_{j_p} \right) = \det(\delta^{i_a}_{j_b}). \]

    For a decomposable \(p\)-vector, the natural pairing is defined by

    \begin{equation} \alpha(X_1\wedge\cdots\wedge X_p) = \alpha(X_1,\ldots,X_p). \end{equation}

    Using this, one shows

    \begin{equation} g(\alpha ,\beta )=g(\alpha ^{\#},\beta ^{\#}). \end{equation}

    This coincides with

    \begin{equation} \langle\alpha,\beta\rangle = \frac1{p!} g^{i_1j_1}\cdots g^{i_pj_p} \alpha_{i_1\cdots i_p} \beta_{j_1\cdots j_p}. \end{equation}

    Proposition
    Edit

    Let \(\alpha \) be \(1\)-form, then

    \[ \la \alpha \wedge \omega , \eta \ra= \la \omega , \iota _{\alpha ^{\#}} \eta \ra \]

    for forms \(\omega \) and \(\eta \) of the appropriate degrees.

    Proof
    Edit

    The components of the \((p+1)\)-form \(\alpha\wedge\omega\) are

    \[ (\alpha\wedge\omega)_{i_0\cdots i_p} = \sum_{a=0}^p(-1)^a \alpha_{i_a} \omega_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_a}\cdots i_p}. \]

    By definition of the inner product on \((p+1)\)-forms,

    \[ \begin{aligned} \langle\alpha\wedge\omega,\eta\rangle = \frac1{(p+1)!} (\alpha\wedge\omega)_{i_0\cdots i_p} \eta_{i_0\cdots i_p}. \end{aligned} \]

    Thus,

    \[ \begin{aligned} \langle\alpha\wedge\omega,\eta\rangle = \frac1{(p+1)!} \sum_{a=0}^p(-1)^a \alpha_{i_a} \omega_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_a}\cdots i_p} \eta_{i_0\cdots i_p}. \end{aligned} \tag{5} \]

    Because \(\eta\) is antisymmetric, moving \(i_a\) to the first position introduces precisely the sign \((-1)^a\). Therefore, after relabeling dummy indices, each summand in (5) has the same value:

    \[ (-1)^a \alpha_{i_a} \omega_{i_0\cdots\widehat{i_a}\cdots i_p} \eta_{i_0\cdots i_p} \quad\leadsto\quad \alpha_j\omega_{i_1\cdots i_p}\eta_{j i_1\cdots i_p}. \]

    There are \(p+1\) such summands. Hence,

    \[ \begin{aligned} \langle\alpha\wedge\omega,\eta\rangle &= \frac{p+1}{(p+1)!} \alpha_j\omega_{i_1\cdots i_p} \eta_{j i_1\cdots i_p}\\ &= \frac1{p!} \alpha_j\omega_{i_1\cdots i_p} \eta_{j i_1\cdots i_p}. \end{aligned} \]

    Since our coframe is orthonormal,

    \[ \alpha^\sharp=\alpha_j e_j. \]

    The definition of interior multiplication gives

    \[ \begin{aligned} (\iota_{\alpha^\sharp}\eta)_{i_1\cdots i_p} &= \eta(\alpha^\sharp,e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_p})\\ &= \alpha_j\eta_{j i_1\cdots i_p}. \end{aligned} \]

    Thus,

    \[ \begin{aligned} \langle\omega,\iota_{\alpha^\sharp}\eta\rangle &= \frac1{p!} \omega_{i_1\cdots i_p} (\iota_{\alpha^\sharp}\eta)_{i_1\cdots i_p}\\ &= \frac1{p!} \omega_{i_1\cdots i_p} \alpha_j\eta_{j i_1\cdots i_p}. \end{aligned} \]

    For an \(E\)-valued \(p\)-form \(\sigma\), the covariant exterior derivative is defined by

    \[ \begin{aligned} (d^\nabla\sigma)(X_0,\ldots,X_p) ={}& \sum_{j=0}^p(-1)^j \nabla^E_{X_j} \sigma(X_0,\ldots,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_p)\\ &+ \sum_{0\le j<k\le p}(-1)^{j+k} \sigma([X_j,X_k],X_0,\ldots,\widehat X_j,\ldots,\widehat X_k,\ldots,X_p). \end{aligned} \tag{8.1} \]

    Because the Levi-Civita connection has zero torsion, the expression simplifies to

    \[ (d^\nabla\sigma)(X_0,\ldots,X_p) = \sum_{j=0}^p(-1)^j (\nabla_{X_j}\sigma) (X_0,\ldots,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_p). \]

    By the definition of the formal adjoint,

    \[ \int_M \langle d^\nabla\omega,\sigma\rangle\,dv_g = \int_M \langle\omega,\delta^\nabla\sigma\rangle\,dv_g. \]

    Lemma
    Edit

    If \((E_i)\) is a basis of \(T_xM\), \(X_j\) are vectors at \(x\), and \(g^{st}\) is the inverse of the matrix \(g(E_s,E_t)\), then for \(\rho\in A^p(\xi)\),

    \[ (\delta^\nabla\rho)(X_1,\ldots,X_{p-1}) = -\sum_{s,t} g^{st} (\nabla_{E_t}\rho) (E_s,X_1,\ldots,X_{p-1}). \]

    In particular, if \(\rho\in A^1(\xi)\), then

    \[ \delta^\nabla\rho = -\operatorname{trace}\nabla\rho. \]

    Now we can give the following example.

    Example (bundle-valued forms)
    Edit

    Let \(E\to M\) be a Euclidean vector bundle with metric connection \(\nabla^E\) and \(\cS=\Lambda^\bullet T^*M\otimes E\), with the connection induced by the Levi-Civita connection and \(\nabla^E\), and

    \[ c(\alpha)\sigma=\alpha\wedge\sigma-\iota_{\alpha^\sharp}\sigma . \]

    Since \((\alpha\wedge)^*=\iota_{\alpha^\sharp}\) and

    \[\alpha\wedge\iota_{\beta^\sharp}+\iota_{\beta^\sharp}\alpha\wedge=g(\alpha,\beta),\]

    while

    \[(\alpha\wedge)^2=0=(\iota_{\alpha^\sharp})^2,\]

    conditions (a)-(b) hold; (c) holds because wedge and interior products are parallel. Since the Levi-Civita connection is torsion free,

    \[ d^\nabla\sigma=\sum_i e^i\wedge\nabla_{e_i}\sigma,\qquad \delta^\nabla\sigma:=(d^\nabla)^*\sigma=-\sum_i\iota_{e_i}\nabla_{e_i}\sigma , \]

    so \(D=d^\nabla+\delta^\nabla\). For \(\sigma\) of pure degree \(p\), \(d^\nabla\sigma\) and \(\delta^\nabla\sigma\) have degrees \(p+1\) and \(p-1\), hence are pointwise orthogonal:

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:pyth} |D\sigma|^2=|d^\nabla\sigma|^2+|\delta^\nabla\sigma|^2 . \end{equation}

    For \(E\) the trivial line bundle this is the operator \(d+d^*\) of [EL78].

    Example
    Edit

    Other Dirac bundles: the spinor bundle of a spin manifold (with the spin Dirac operator), twisted by any bundle with metric connection; on a Kähler manifold, \(\Lambda^{0,\bullet}T^*M\otimes E\) for a Hermitian holomorphic bundle with its Chern connection, with \(D=\sqrt2(\bar\partial_E+\bar\partial_E^*)\) [LM89, Ch. II].

    Here is the form of the theorem we prove.

    \begin{thmA} Let \(\cS\) be a Dirac bundle over a connected Riemannian manifold \(M\), and let \(u\in W^{1,2}_\loc(M;\cS)\) satisfy

    \begin{equation}\label{eq:hyp} |Du|\le V\,|u|\qquad\text{a.e. on }M, \end{equation}

    for some \(V\in L^\infty_\loc(M)\). If \(u=0\) a.e.\ on a nonempty open subset of \(M\), then \(u=0\) a.e.\ on \(M\). \end{thmA}

    By Example~?? and \eqref{eq:pyth}, Theorem~A contains the statement of [EL78, (1.27)], with forms allowed to take values in a bundle:

    \begin{thmB}[Aronszajn--Krzywicki--Szarski] Let \(M\) be a connected Riemannian manifold, \(E\to M\) a Riemannian vector bundle with metric connection, and \(\sigma\in W^{1,2}_\loc(\Lambda^pT^*M\otimes E)\). Suppose that for every compact \(K\subset M\) there is a constant \(C_K\) with

    \[ |d^\nabla\sigma|^2+|\delta^\nabla\sigma|^2\le C_K|\sigma|^2\qquad\text{a.e. on }K. \]

    If \(\sigma\) vanishes on a nonempty open subset of \(M\), then \(\sigma\equiv0\). \end{thmB}

    Remark
    Edit

    1. Both \(d\) and \(d^*\) are needed. If \(f\in C^\infty_c(M)\) is nonconstant, \(\sigma=df\) is closed and vanishes outside \(\supp f\). Likewise \(\sigma={*}df\) is coclosed. What makes the theorem work is that \(D^2\) has the scalar principal symbol \(|\xi|^2\); see the Weitzenböck formula \eqref{eq:weitz}.

    2. No regularity of the potential. Only \(V\in L^\infty_\loc\) is used. This is what allows nonlinear applications (§ ??).

    3. Strong unique continuation. For smooth metrics the stronger conclusion also holds when \(u\) only vanishes to infinite order at a point (in the \(L^2\) sense); this requires Carleman estimates with weights singular at a point and is considerably more delicate for first-order systems. The weak form is all that is used in [EL78], and it is what we prove.
